name: New Beat
summary: New Beat was a short-lived but highly influential electronic music genre and subculture that originated in Belgium in the late 1980s, flourishing between 1987 and 1989.
description:
New Beat was a short-lived but highly influential electronic music genre and subculture that originated in Belgium in the late 1980s, flourishing between 1987 and 1989. The genre's signature sound was created by accident when a DJ began playing 45 RPM records (typically dark and heavy EBM and New Wave tracks) at the slower 33 RPM speed, resulting in a dark, hypnotic, and mid-tempo beat.

The subculture was centered in Belgian nightclubs such as Boccaccio, where its eclectic and androgynous fashion style developed. The look was a unique mix of cycling shorts, BDSM-inspired leather gear, religious iconography, and quirky accessories like the "Bomma badge" (brooches made from repurposed gravestone portraits).

While it emerged concurrently with Acid House in the UK, New Beat had a distinctly darker and slower industrial edge, and it is considered a European precursor to the wider rave movement and harder electronic genres like Hardcore Techno and Gabber .
culturalContext: Key values (per the Aesthetics Wiki): Hedonism, experimentation, underground club culture, androgyny, dark humor

fashion.Overview: A fashion guide for New Beat (c. 1988), demonstrating the aesthetic's elements: cropped frayed denim, high-waisted black trousers, and the pervasive use of Smiley face iconography associated with Acid House influence. New Beat fashion was an extravagant and often androgynous style that complemented the dark, hypnotic mood of the music. It was largely codified by designer Idriz Jossa and his "New Beat Fashion" collection created at the Antwerp Fashion Academy.
fashion.Iconography and Subversion: Nikkie Van Lierop of the band 101 wearing the "New Beat Fashion" look in a live performance, featuring the bomma badge on the sleeves. The New Beat subcultural uniform had three unique symbols: first, the "Bomma badge," an oval ceramic pin resembling a portrait found on gravestones ( bomma being a colloquial term for grandmother).
